title: Redis Atomicity: Pipelines, Transactions & Lua
summary: A dense field guide to executing multiple Redis commands as one unit — pipelining for throughput, MULTI/EXEC for batching, WATCH for optimistic locking, and Lua/Functions for true server-side atomicity. Covers the mechanics, the guarantees Redis actually gives you, the trade-offs, and the mistakes that silently break correctness.

chapters.title: The Round-Trip Problem
points: Redis is a single-threaded command executor with a networked request/response protocol (RESP)
Every command costs one RTT: client sends, blocks, server replies — latency dominates, not CPU
100k SET commands at 0.5ms RTT = ~50 seconds of pure waiting, even though Redis executes each in ~1µs
Throughput ceiling of naive clients ≈ 1/RTT, independent of how fast Redis is
Local socket RTT ~30-50µs; same-datacenter ~200µs-1ms; cross-region 50ms+ — the gap defines the fix
Three distinct problems people conflate: latency (pipelines), grouping (MULTI/EXEC), and read-modify-write races (WATCH or Lua)
Pipelining solves latency only — it gives no atomicity
MULTI/EXEC solves grouping and isolation — it gives no conditional logic
Lua/Functions solve read-modify-write — server-side branching on values read in the same execution
Redis is single-threaded for command execution, so every command is already atomic by itself: INCR, SETNX, LPUSH need no transaction
Redis 6+ has threaded I/O (io-threads) for socket read/write, but command execution stays on one thread
The mental model: Redis executes one command at a time from a queue; your job is deciding how commands enter that queue
Compare: `redis-cli --latency` measures RTT; `redis-benchmark -P 16` measures pipelined throughput
Rule of thumb: if you need speed reach for pipeline; if you need correctness reach for Lua

chapters.title: Pipelining Mechanics
points: Pipelining = write N requests to the socket without waiting, then read N replies in order
RESP replies come back in exactly the order commands were sent — the client matches by position, not by ID
Code: `p = r.pipeline(transaction=False); p.set('a',1); p.incr('b'); p.execute()` (redis-py)
Typical speedup 5-10x; a 100k-command load can drop from ~50s to ~2s
Pipeline is a CLIENT-side technique — Redis needs no special support beyond its input buffer
Batch size matters: 100-1000 commands per flush is the sweet spot
Batching too large blows the server output buffer and spikes memory; each queued reply is held until you read
`client-output-buffer-limit normal 0 0 0` means unlimited for normal clients — a huge pipeline can OOM the server
Pipelined commands are NOT atomic: other clients' commands can interleave between them
No conditional logic: you cannot branch on reply #3 to decide command #4 — all commands are chosen before any reply arrives
Errors do not stop a pipeline: command 4 failing still runs commands 5..N; you inspect per-command replies
Pipelining works with any command mix, including reads — a pipeline of GETs is a legitimate multi-get
Cluster caveat: keys must be split per-node; client libraries shard the pipeline and merge replies
Anti-pattern: pipelining inside a loop with an execute() per iteration — that's just RTT with extra steps

chapters.title: MULTI / EXEC: The Transaction Block
points: MULTI opens a transaction; subsequent commands are QUEUED not executed; EXEC runs them all
Server replies `+QUEUED` to each command inside MULTI — the reply is not the command's result
EXEC returns an array of replies, one per queued command, in order
DISCARD aborts: flushes the queue, exits MULTI state, returns +OK
Guarantee 1 — isolation: no other client's command runs between the first and last command of EXEC
Guarantee 2 — all-or-nothing queuing: if any command fails to queue, EXEC aborts everything
Redis transactions are serialized and atomic in execution, but they are NOT ACID-with-rollback
Nested MULTI is an error: `ERR MULTI calls can not be nested`
Commands inside MULTI cannot see each other's results — no branching, no reading a value to decide the next write
`redis-py`'s default `r.pipeline()` wraps in MULTI/EXEC; pass `transaction=False` for a raw pipeline
Client libraries usually pipeline the MULTI...EXEC block too, so the whole transaction is one RTT
MULTI does NOT block other clients before EXEC — the queue is per-connection, the server keeps serving everyone
A transaction of independent writes (SET a, SET b, INCR c) is the ideal use case
If you find yourself wanting an `if` inside MULTI, you actually need Lua

chapters.title: Errors Inside Transactions (No Rollback)
points: Two error classes, two very different behaviors — this is the #1 misunderstanding
Class 1 — queue-time error: unknown command, wrong arity, OOM. Detected at queue time
Queue-time error makes Redis reply with an error instead of +QUEUED and flag the transaction dirty
EXEC on a dirty transaction returns `EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of previous errors.` — zero commands run
Class 2 — runtime error: correct syntax, wrong type, e.g. `LPUSH` on a string key
Runtime errors are NOT detected at queue time — the command queues fine
On EXEC, a runtime error appears as one error entry in the reply array; every OTHER command still executes and stays applied
There is NO ROLLBACK: Redis will not undo the commands that succeeded
Rationale from Redis docs: runtime errors come from programming bugs detectable in dev; rollback machinery would cost speed and simplicity
Practical consequence: you must inspect every element of the EXEC reply array, not just check that EXEC didn't throw
Redis < 2.6.5 did not even detect queue-time errors — EXEC executed the valid subset
Example: MULTI; SET k v; LPUSH k x; INCR n; EXEC → replies [OK, WRONGTYPE error, 1]; k and n are both modified
Compare to SQL: `BEGIN/ROLLBACK` undoes partial work; Redis has no undo log at all
Design defense: validate types and inputs before queueing, or move the logic into Lua where you control the flow
Lua does not give you rollback either — an error mid-script leaves earlier writes applied

chapters.title: WATCH and Optimistic Locking
points: WATCH key [key ...] marks keys for check-and-set; EXEC fails if any watched key changed
Optimistic concurrency control: assume no conflict, detect it at commit, retry on failure
Failed EXEC returns a Null reply (nil), NOT an error — a missing check is a silent bug
The full loop: WATCH key → GET key (read outside MULTI) → compute in client → MULTI → SET new → EXEC → retry if nil
WATCH must come BEFORE the read, or you race between reading and watching
UNWATCH clears all watches on the connection; EXEC and DISCARD also clear them implicitly
Redis flags dirty on any modification of the key — including by the same client, expiry, or eviction
It is value-blind: SET k same-value still trips the watch (Redis ≥ 6.0.9 tracks touch not value change)
Key deletion or a DEL then re-create trips the watch; so does FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB
Worked example — atomic ZPOP: WATCH zset; element = ZRANGE zset 0 0; MULTI; ZREM zset element; EXEC; retry on nil
Worked example — INCR without INCR: WATCH k; v = GET k; MULTI; SET k v+1; EXEC
Retry loop needs a bounded attempt count plus jittered backoff or you spin forever under contention
Livelock hazard: N clients watching one hot key means most EXECs fail; throughput collapses as N grows
Optimistic (WATCH) vs pessimistic (a SET NX lock): WATCH has no lock to leak, but degrades badly under contention
WATCH is per-connection state — a connection-pooling client that hands you a different socket breaks the whole scheme
In Redis Cluster all watched keys must hash to the same slot as the transaction's keys

chapters.title: Lua Scripting: EVAL and the Script Cache
points: EVAL script numkeys key [key ...] arg [arg ...] — numkeys splits KEYS from ARGV
KEYS and ARGV are 1-indexed Lua tables: KEYS[1], ARGV[1]
Always pass keys via KEYS, never hardcode them — Redis Cluster and future proxies route by declared keys
redis.call(...) raises a Lua error that aborts the script; redis.pcall(...) returns an error table you can inspect
Return with `return` — a script with no return yields nil to the client
SCRIPT LOAD returns the SHA1; EVALSHA sha numkeys ... runs the cached script with a much smaller payload
Standard client pattern: try EVALSHA, catch `NOSCRIPT`, fall back to EVAL, cache the SHA
Script cache is not persisted: it is lost on restart, on SCRIPT FLUSH, and on failover to a fresh replica
Example — atomic compare-and-delete lock release: `if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`
Example — rate limiter: `local c=redis.call('incr',KEYS[1]); if c==1 then redis.call('expire',KEYS[1],ARGV[1]) end; return c`
Type conversion Lua→Redis: number is truncated to integer (3.7 becomes 3), true→1, false→nil
Type conversion Redis→Lua: bulk string→Lua string, nil reply→false, status reply→table with `ok` field
Lua tables convert to arrays and STOP at the first nil element — a sparse table silently truncates
Return a table `{err='msg'}` to produce a client-visible error, `{ok='status'}` for a status reply
Redis 7 adds Redis Functions (FUNCTION LOAD, FCALL) — named, persisted, replicated libraries instead of ephemeral SHAs

chapters.title: Script Atomicity, Blocking & Determinism
points: A script runs atomically: Redis blocks all other clients for the full duration — the strongest guarantee available
Corollary: a slow script is a server-wide stall; a loop over a million keys freezes every other client
busy-reply-threshold (formerly lua-time-limit), default 5000ms: after it, Redis replies BUSY to other clients
BUSY state accepts only SCRIPT KILL and SHUTDOWN NOSAVE
SCRIPT KILL only works if the script has not yet written; after a write the only escape is SHUTDOWN NOSAVE and data loss
Keep scripts short — target sub-millisecond; do not implement a batch job in Lua
Determinism mattered historically: pre-Redis-7 verbatim replication forbade nondeterminism, so scripts saw a fixed TIME and a seeded random
redis.replicate_commands() (Redis 3.2+) switched to effects replication; Redis 7 makes effects replication the only mode
Effects replication ships the resulting write commands to replicas and the AOF, not the script text — so nondeterminism is now safe
Legacy hazard to recognize in old code: a script using math.random or os.time under verbatim replication diverged replicas
Shebang flags (Redis 7): `#!lua name=mylib` for functions, `no-writes` to mark a script read-only so it can run on replicas
no-writes scripts are also allowed during a write-blocked state (e.g. replica-read or OOM)
Global variable writes are blocked — the sandbox errors on `x = 1`; use `local x = 1`
Available libraries: cjson, cmsgpack, bit, struct, redis.sha1hex, redis.breakpoint (debug)
redis.log(redis.LOG_WARNING, msg) writes to the Redis log for debugging
No network, no os.execute, no require — the sandbox is deliberately sealed

chapters.title: Choosing the Right Tool
points: Comparison row — Pipeline: atomic NO, isolated NO, conditional NO, RTT 1, blocking none. Use for bulk throughput
Comparison row — MULTI/EXEC: atomic YES, isolated YES, conditional NO, RTT 1 (pipelined), blocking during EXEC. Use for a fixed batch of writes
Comparison row — WATCH+MULTI: atomic YES, conditional YES (client-side), RTT 2+ and retries. Use for low-contention read-modify-write
Comparison row — Lua/EVAL: atomic YES, conditional YES (server-side), RTT 1, blocking for the script's duration. Use for read-modify-write on hot keys
Decision rule: no reads involved → pipeline. Fixed writes → MULTI. Branch on a value → Lua
Prefer a single native command when one exists: INCR, SETNX, GETSET, SET k v NX EX 30, LMOVE, ZADD GT
SET key val NX EX ttl replaces the old SETNX+EXPIRE pair and its crash-between-commands bug
Lua beats WATCH under contention: no retries, no wasted RTTs, no livelock — one pass, always succeeds
WATCH beats Lua when the computation is expensive or needs data Redis doesn't have (an external API, heavy math)
Lua beats WATCH for correctness-critical paths because the check and the write cannot be separated
Cost of Lua: harder to debug, harder to test, script cache management, blocks the server
Cost of WATCH: retry loops, contention sensitivity, connection-affinity requirements
Complexity: pipeline O(N) commands with 1 RTT; WATCH loop is O(N × retries) RTTs; Lua is 1 RTT with server-side O(work)
Redis 7 Functions are the modern home for anything you'd otherwise ship as a long-lived EVALSHA

chapters.title: Common Mistakes
points: Assuming MULTI rolls back on a runtime error — it does not; partial effects persist
Ignoring the nil reply from EXEC after WATCH, so a lost race silently becomes a lost update
Reading a value inside MULTI and expecting the value — you get +QUEUED, and the real reply only at EXEC
Using a connection pool with WATCH, so the WATCH and the EXEC land on different connections
Hardcoding key names in Lua instead of using KEYS — breaks Redis Cluster with CROSSSLOT
Cross-slot transactions in Cluster: all keys in one MULTI/EXEC or script must hash to one slot; use hash tags `{user:1}:name`
Long-running Lua scripts stalling the entire server, then discovering SCRIPT KILL is useless after a write
Using KEYS * inside a script — O(N) over the whole keyspace while everything else is blocked
Building a distributed lock with SETNX then EXPIRE as two commands: a crash between them leaks the lock forever
Releasing someone else's lock with a bare DEL instead of a Lua compare-and-delete on the owner token
Assuming EXEC is durable: it is atomic in memory, but not fsynced unless appendfsync always is set
Assuming replicas are consistent after EXEC — replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose acknowledged transactions
Pipelining a million commands in one flush and OOMing the server's output buffer
Watching a key that a TTL will expire, then blaming Redis when EXEC returns nil
Relying on Lua's implicit float truncation: returning 3.7 gives the client 3
Returning a Lua table with a nil hole and losing every element after it

chapters.title: Guarantees, Durability & Recap
points: What Redis atomicity means precisely: no interleaving of other clients' commands, single-threaded serial execution
What it does NOT mean: no rollback, no snapshot isolation across separate transactions, no cross-key durability barrier
Durability is orthogonal: RDB snapshots lose recent writes; AOF everysec loses up to 1s; appendfsync always is durable but slow
A successful EXEC only guarantees the commands ran in memory on the primary
Replication is asynchronous by default — an acknowledged EXEC can be lost on failover
WAIT numreplicas timeout blocks until N replicas acknowledge; it improves the odds but is not a consensus protocol
Redis Cluster gives no cross-slot atomicity at all — plan the key layout with hash tags up front
Persistence of code: EVAL scripts live in an ephemeral cache; Redis 7 Functions persist in RDB/AOF and replicate
Cheat sheet — MULTI/EXEC/DISCARD/WATCH/UNWATCH; EVAL/EVALSHA/SCRIPT LOAD/SCRIPT FLUSH/SCRIPT KILL; FUNCTION LOAD/FCALL
Testing checklist: assert on every element of an EXEC array, simulate a concurrent writer to exercise the WATCH-nil path, benchmark script duration
Observability: SLOWLOG catches slow scripts; INFO commandstats breaks down EVAL cost; LATENCY DOCTOR flags fork and script stalls
Default reach order: native single command > Lua/Function > MULTI/EXEC > WATCH loop > pipeline for throughput only
One-line summary: pipeline for speed, MULTI for grouping, WATCH for optimism, Lua for certainty
Final warning: atomic is not durable, and single-node atomic is not distributed atomic
